scenario.customer: Private limited company operating one hand car wash site. Business current account opened for takings, wages and supplier payments.
scenario.alert: Cash credited in the last 90 days is several times the level expected from the customer profile.
scenario.priorWork: Customer is a car wash, so some cash is expected. Cash value is higher than the profile. Escalated for full review.

documents.document: One site with three employees. Expected annual turnover GBP 165,000, of which about 40% in cash. No international payments expected.
Incorporated in 2025. One director, who also holds 100% of the shares. The director is also listed as a director of Fictia Lettings Ltd.
Cash is paid in by three different people, often on consecutive days. Several deposits were made at branches more than 40 miles from the car wash.
One-page unaudited summary. Average price per wash GBP 12. The site has two bays and opens seven days a week. No till records or daily takings sheets were supplied.

The director says trade increased because of good weather. The payments to Exampleland are described as parts bought for a relative's business. The management charge is described as head office costs. No invoices were supplied.
Water supplier invoice for the quarter. The site's metered use is consistent with about 25 washes a day.

reportBlocks.block: The company deposited a lot of cash during the quarter and also made several payments.

Over the 90-day review period, cash credited to the company's account was several times the level declared at onboarding. It was paid in by three individuals, including at branches far from the site. Most of the funds were then sent to a connected company and to a company overseas.
The director could not give a satisfactory explanation, which proves that the funds are criminal proceeds.

The cash cannot be reconciled with the business. The declared price, site capacity, payroll and water use all point to much lower takings. Funds moved on to a company connected to the director and to an overseas company for goods that do not fit a car wash, and no invoices were supplied.
Car washes are a high-risk sector, so the cash in this account is likely to be criminal.
The director was told that a report would be made, so that the missing invoices could be provided.
The case was referred to the MLRO with the supporting documents. The customer has not been told about the referral.
A defence is requested so that the account can continue to operate normally.

answer.explanation: Cash is expected at a car wash, but not at this level. At GBP 12 per wash the deposits imply more than 100 washes a day, while the water bill points to about 25. Payroll and card receipts are also small compared with the cash. The money then leaves for a company connected to the director and for an overseas company, with no invoices. No specific payment is awaiting a decision, so this case needs a SAR rather than a DAML.

irregularity.note: Cash credits are several times the level declared at onboarding.
Large regular payments go to a company connected to the director, with no supporting agreement.
International payments were not expected, and vehicle parts do not fit a car wash.
Several people pay in cash, including at branches far from the site.
The price and two-bay site cannot support the cash banked, and no till records were supplied.
Water use points to far fewer washes than the cash implies.
